learning_outcomes.text: Have knowledge and understanding of the principles of single-variable calculus that underlie the branch of industrial engineering.
Be able to apply their knowledge and understanding to identify, formulate and solve single-variable calculus problems using established methods.
Be able to select and use appropriate tools and methods to solve single-variable calculus problems.
Be able to combine theory and practice to solve single-variable calculus problems.
Understand the methods and procedures of single-variable calculus, their area of application and their limitations.
Knowledge and understanding of the scientific and mathematical principles that underlie their branch of engineering.
The ability to apply their knowledge and understanding to identify, formulate and solve engineering problems using established methods.
The ability to select and use appropriate equipment, tools and methods.
The ability to combine theory and practice to solve engineering problems.

That students have demonstrated possession and understanding of knowledge in a field of study that builds on general secondary education, and is usually found at a level that, while supported by advanced textbooks, also includes some aspects that imply knowledge from the forefront of their field of study.

That students know how to apply their knowledge to their work or vocation in a professional manner and possess the competences that are usually demonstrated through the elaboration and defense of arguments and the resolution of problems within their field of study.
Ability to solve problems with initiative, decision-making, creativity, critical reasoning and to communicate and transmit knowledge, skills and abilities in the field of Industrial Engineering.

Ability to solve mathematical problems that may arise in engineering. Aptitude to apply knowledge of: linear algebra; geometry; differential geometry; differential and integral calculus; differential and partial differential equations; numerical methods; numerical algorithms; statistics and optimization.

syllabus_topics: The real line, sets of numbers, inequalities, absolute value, intervals and sets in the plane
Sequences of numbers and fundamental concepts. Recurrent sequences. Limits of sequences, Stirling's Formula and Stoltz's Criterion
Series of numbers, fundamental concepts. Convergence criteria for series of positive numbers, absolute convergence, conditional convergence and Leibniz's criterion
Elementary functions, elementary transformations, composition of functions and inverse function. Polar coordinates
Limits of functions, definition and fundamental theorems. Calculation of limits
Continuity of functions, properties and fundamental theorems
Differentiation of functions. Definitions, differentiation rules, derivatives of elementary functions, meaning of the derivative
Bernoulli-L'Hôpital's Rule. Basic theorems on differentiation
Optimization problems of two-variable functions subject to a condition
Convexity and asymptotes. Graphs of functions
Taylor polynomial and series, definition, properties and examples. Calculation of limits with the Taylor polynomial
Interval of convergence of a Taylor series
Calculation of primitives: immediate integrals, integration by parts, by decomposition into simple fractions, change of variable and other integration methods
Definite integral and fundamental theorems of calculus. Geometric and physical applications of the definite integral
assessment_rules: The ordinary final grade is composed of the sum of the scores from the ordinary final exam (60%) and the two partial evaluation controls (40% total, 20% each). The extraordinary final exam has a value of 100%. The extraordinary final grade is the maximum between the score obtained in the extraordinary final exam and the sum of the scores from the three partial evaluation controls plus 60% of the score obtained in the extraordinary final exam. Oral tests may be conducted to ensure the acquisition of learning outcomes.
